title: Ananias (Acts 9:10–19)
hookLine: a frightened believer is sent to heal his enemy and calls him "brother Saul"

cards: Here's a job nobody would volunteer for: knock on the door of the one person in town you're most afraid of. Not to argue. To help.

That job goes to a man named Ananias, an ordinary follower of Jesus in Damascus, not an apostle; almost nothing else is known about him. In a vision the Lord calls his name, and he answers, here I am.
The instructions are specific: go to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul.
He's praying, and he's seen a vision of a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him so he can see again. Ananias knows who Saul is.

teach.h: LORD, I HAVE HEARD OF THIS MAN.
teach.b: So Ananias objects. In the King James Bible: "Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem." And he came here with papers to arrest us.
I like that he says it; the Bible keeps many honest objections.
The answer comes back: go, "for he is a chosen vessel unto me." Not, he's harmless. Just, go.
So he walks the street called Straight and into the room where the man the believers dread sits blind.
He lays his hands on him, and his first words are these: "Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me." Brother.
Before Saul has done a single thing to earn it, before anyone knows if he's for real. The man who came to take Ananias away in chains is greeted as family.
Then, Luke says, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see.
That's where the English saying comes from: the scales fell from my eyes. He gets up, is baptized, and eats, for the first time in three days.
The well-known one here is Saul, who'll become Paul, whose letters are in the New Testament.
But Paul's sight comes back through the hands of a man Acts names in only two places, who was scared, said so, and went anyway. His first two words are today's line.

how: Christians in many churches call one another brother and sister, a habit that goes back to the first believers. Ananias of Damascus is honored as a saint in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

games.q: you're Ananias. you've just laid your hands on the man who came to arrest you. what is your first word to him?
games.why: brother saul, the Lord, even Jesus, hath sent me. family first, before Saul has earned anything.

practice: Bring to mind someone you keep at a distance: not someone dangerous, just someone you've quietly decided isn't one of us, a neighbor, a relative, a coworker on the other side of some argument.
Say their name in your head with brother or sister in front of it, and notice what happens in you: resistance, maybe, or a softening. If you pray, you can pray for them by that name.

wordCard.voice: Ananias. The frightened disciple in Damascus who went anyway, laid his hands on his enemy, and called him brother.

orig.note: Greek: brother, literally from the same womb. The first Christians used it for one another.

carryVoice: Your line: brother saul. Next, a rooftop vision and a Roman's door. See you tomorrow.
